Learning Objectives
Understand the typical clinical presentation of gout.
Specify the risk factors associated with gout.
Identify typical diagnostic findings, including bloodwork and joint aspiration findings.
Understand the available medication and treatment options.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Gout is a metabolic disorder manifested by uric acid crystals in the synovium.
Prevalence is increasing
Involvement of a single joint is common.
The first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint is the most common joint involved.1


Overview
Gout is a common type of inflammatory arthritis characterized by deposition of
monosodium urate crystals. It affects nearly 4% of adults in the United States.1 Its clinical
manifestations arise as a result of the body’s inflammatory response to the crystals.
Although acute therapies focus on decreasing inflammation, successful long-term
management centers on reduction of serum urate levels.
Gout arises in the setting of hyperuricemia, which occurs because of overproduction or
underexcretion of urate. After serum urate levels rise above a critical concentration,
depositions of monosodium urate crystals can occur. These may or may not be
symptomatic. Acute gout flares represent an inflammatory response to these crystal
depositions. Long-term manifestations of chronic gout include tophi, radiographic
erosions, and gouty arthritis.
Epidemiology and Risk Factors
Gout typically affects older men and postmenopausal women.
Comorbidities are common in patients with gout, particularly hypertension, chronic kidney
disease, obesity, and diabetes mellitus.
Foods associated with gout flares include alcohol, red meat, sugary beverages, and seafood.
Acute illness or surgical management also can precipitate gout flares.

Epidemiology and Risk Factors
The most obvious risk factor for gout is hyperuricemia. Risk factors that are associated
with hyperuricemia are consequently risk factors for gout. These include older age, male
sex, and ethnicity. Certain foods also are associated with elevated urate concentrations,
including alcohol, red meat, sugary beverages, and seafood. Research has shown that
consumption of alcohol and red meat are associated with recurrent gout flares. Although
men are at increased risk for gout relative to women, the risk for women increases after
menopause.1 Relative to White patients, a higher prevalence of gout has been noted in

certain minority populations, particularly Black patients, Hmong Chinese in the United
States, and Maoris in New Zealand.2
Comorbidities are common in patients with gout, particularly hypertension, chronic
kidney disease, obesity, and diabetes mellitus. More than 50% of patients with gout are
obese.1 Patients with gout have an increased risk of death, most notably from
cardiovascular disease. Certain medications also have been associated with higher gout
incidence, most notably diuretics.1
In as many as 44% of patients with a history of gout, surgical treatment can precipitate
an acute gout flare. Flares typically occur 3 to 4 days postoperatively. Interestingly, these
flares more often involve the knee joint or other joints in the foot aside from the first
MTP joint.3
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients typically present with acute onset, atraumatic joint pain.
A thorough patient history should identify risk factors and any history of similar past episodes.

Patient History
Patients with an acute gout flare present with an atraumatic onset of pain, swelling, and
redness. An acute illness, surgical management, dehydration, alcohol use, and
consumption of meat or seafood can precipitate flares.1 Patients should be questioned
about any history of similar flares affecting the same joint or other joints in the body.
Any predisposing risk factors should be identified.
Physical Examination

Involved joints are intensely painful, swollen, and erythematous.

Physical Examination
The affected joint typically is swollen, erythematous, warm, and exquisitely tender to
palpation (Figure 1). Fever is not typical but can occur, particularly during polyarticular
flares.1 Therefore, the presentation of acute gout may be confused with infection. The
first MTP joint, the most common site of involvement, is involved in more than 50% of
patients with gout; however, other sites in the foot and ankle also are common.1,4
Figure 1
Clinical photograph of a foot shows the acute presentation of gout, which includes an
erythematous, swollen, exquisitely painful joint. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is
the most common site involved. (Courtesy of Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
Subcutaneous nodules, tophi, may be identified by the patient or on physical
examination. These lesions are most often painless but can become acutely inflamed.
They also can ulcerate, leading to drainage of their white, chalky contents.

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Periarticular erosions are a classic finding on radiographs.
The peripheral margin of the erosion often has a thin overlying rim of bone (cliff sign).

Radiography
The classic radiographic finding associated with chronic gout is periarticular erosions
(Figure 2). These are observed as bony erosions with overhanging edges (cliff sign) and a
sclerotic rim. Joint-space narrowing also may be observed in the setting of chronic
disease. In patients presenting with an initial flare, radiographs usually are normal.
Figure 2
AP radiograph of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of a patient with chronic gout
demonstrates soft-tissue prominence in the area of a tophus and associated
periarticular erosions (arrow). (Courtesy of Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore, MD.)

Ultrasonography
Characteristic ultrasonography findings associated with gout include the double contour sign
and a snowstorm appearance of hyperechoic foci within a joint.

Ultrasonography
Gout has certain typical characteristics on ultrasonography that may aid in diagnosis.
Advantages of ultrasonography are its low cost, widespread availability, and lack of
radiation of exposure. Urate deposits can be observed as hyperechoic enhancements at
the articular surface (the double contour sign), as floating hyperechoic foci within a joint
(snowstorm appearance), or as hyperechoic aggregates in patients with tophi. The
double contour sign, in particular, is more than 80% specific for a diagnosis of gout and
is one of the diagnostic criteria included in the 2015 American College of
Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism Classification Criteria for Gout.5,6
Computed Tomography
Dual-energy CT can identify monosodium urate deposits and, therefore, help differentiate gout
from other inflammatory arthropathies.

Computed Tomography
Dual-energy CT can identify urate deposition in and surrounding joints. By obtaining
images acquired at two different energy levels, urate deposits can be effectively
differentiated from calcium deposits. This may aid in differentiating gout from other
inflammatory arthropathies. The sensitivity and specificity for detection of monosodium
urate deposits on dual-energy CT scans are good to excellent, ranging from 78% to
100%.7 However, sensitivity is lower in patients with early disease.5
Along with ultrasonography and radiography, the finding of urate deposits via dual-
energy CT is among the imaging criteria for diagnosis established by the 2015 American

for Gout.6 Studies using dual-energy CT have identified urate deposits in not only joints
but also ligaments and tendons, with the Achilles tendon being most commonly
affected.7
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI findings typically are nonspecific and are not as useful as other imaging modalities for
diagnosis.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI typically is not used for diagnosis of gout; however, it often is used to evaluate soft-
tissue masses of unknown etiology, which may include gouty tophi, and it may be useful
for surgical planning. Gouty tophi typically appear as low-to-intermediate signal masses
on T1- and T2-weighted images (Figure 3). Homogeneous enhancement is most typical;
however, peripheral enhancement also may be observed. During an acute flare,
nonspecific edema, synovitis, and joint effusions typically are observed.8

Pathology
Gout is the result of crystallization of uric acid in periarticular soft tissues, which occurs as a
result of hyperuricemia.
Acute gout attacks are the result of an inflammatory response to monosodium urate crystals.

Pathology
Gout arises in the setting of hyperuricemia. Because humans are unable to metabolize
uric acid, most of it is excreted through the kidneys and a smaller amount through the
biliary tract. Hyperuricemia can develop in patients with impaired uric acid excretion or,
to a lesser extent, increased uric acid production. Because of the limited solubility of uric
acid, elevated serum levels of uric acid lead to crystallization of uric acid into
monosodium urate, which tends to accumulate in periarticular soft tissues.
The foot is thought to be the most common site affected by gout because of its
peripheral location, with lower temperatures and pH leading to decreased solubility of
uric acid. If urate crystals trigger a macrophage-initiated inflammatory response, an
acute gout attack is precipitated. Gout does not occur in all patients with
hyperuricemia.1,7
Diagnosis
Joint aspiration is the only definitive diagnostic procedure. Needle- and rod-shaped crystals
with negative birefringence are observed.
Aspirate white blood cell count usually is less than 50,000 to 60,000/μL.
Serum uric acid level often is elevated (but not always).
Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows amorphous material and inflammatory cells.SEND FEEDBACK


Diagnosis
Identification of monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid or tophus contents
definitively establishes a diagnosis of gout. On polarizing light microscopy, negative
birefringent needle-shaped crystals are observed. Synovial fluid appears yellow and
cloudy, with an elevated white cell count consisting predominantly of neutrophils.
An elevated serum uric acid level may aid in diagnosis but is not adequate alone. Most
patients with hyperuricemia do not have gout, and during an acute flare, a patient may
have normal serum uric acid levels. If gout is suspected, serum uric acid should be
retested after the patient has recovered from the flare.1
Inflammatory markers, particularly C-reactive protein level, usually are increased during
a flare; however, this is a nonspecific finding.
Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
An acute gout flare can be mistaken for septic arthritis. Occasionally, both diagnoses
may be present. Synovial fluid should be sent for Gram stain and culture to rule out
infection. Although white cell counts greater than 50,000/μL are more common with
infection, isolated gout also may lead to levels this high.1
Other types of inflammatory arthritis also may be confused with gout, particularly
pseudogout, which is associated with deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate
crystals. Dissimilar to monosodium urate crystals, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate
crystals are observed as positive birefringent crystals under light microscopy.
Management

Nonsurgical Management
NSAIDs are the preferred treatment option for the management of acute gout.
Colchicine also is useful for acute flares.
Hypouricemic therapy, such as allopurinol and probenecid, controls hyperuricemia and
prevent recurrent flares.

Nonsurgical Management
Gout flares are self-limited, typically lasting 1 to 2 weeks. Management should be
initiated as soon as possible. NSAIDs are the preferred of treatment option for the
management of acute flares. Colchicine, a drug with diverse anti-inflammatory effects,
also is useful for the acute management of flares.9 Corticosteroids are useful in patients
with comorbidities, such as kidney disease, that preclude the use of NSAIDs and
colchicine. They can be administered orally or via intra-articular injection. In patients in
whom standard therapies fail, interleukin-1 inhibitors recently have been used to
manage gout flares.10
Unmanaged hyperuricemia after an initial gout flare may lead to recurrent and/or
polyarticular flares. In the long term, without management, chronic gout and gouty tophi
can develop.1 Therefore, long-term urate-lowering therapy is critical in patients with
gout. Recent research has shown that urate-lowering therapy can be initiated during an
acute flare without exacerbating symptoms.
The most common urate-lowering drugs are allopurinol and probenecid. Allopurinol
inhibits urate production, whereas probenecid increases urate excretion. Upon starting
therapy with these drugs, serum urate levels should be monitored frequently, and
dosing should be adjusted accordingly. Research has shown that dose escalation of
allopurinol to achieve a goal serum urate level leads to decreased long-term joint
erosion and fewer acute gout flares.1,11 Low-dose colchicine also can be used for
effective long-term anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.1

Surgeons should be aware that patients with a history of gout who undergo surgical
treatment are less likely to experience a postoperative gout flare if being treated via
allopurinol therapy.3 Gout flares that occur postoperatively can be managed similar to
any other flare, via medications and/or intra-articular steroid injection.
Surgical Management
Surgical treatment may be considered for patients with symptomatic tophi or with end-stage
gouty arthritis.

Surgical Management
The preferred treatment option for the management of gout is medical. For patients in
whom nonsurgical treatment fails, surgical treatment may be considered for the excision
of symptomatic tophi or for the management of gouty arthritis via fusion (Figure 4). For
patients with severe gouty arthritis of the ankle, total ankle replacement may be
considered.12
Figure 4
Photograph of gross pathology after tophus excision from a first metatarsophalangeal
joint shows characteristic chalky white material. (Courtesy of Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore,
MD.)

Limited reports have been published on the surgical management of gouty arthritis. In a
small case series, patients who underwent first MTP fusion had substantially better
outcomes than patients who underwent isolated tophus excision. Isolated tophus
excision led to persistent symptoms and progression of arthritis in 6 of 9 patients.13
Conversely, a small study on arthroscopic débridement of the first MTP joint in patients
with chronic gout reported substantially improved function and fewer gout attacks after
treatment.14
Although severe ankle arthritis secondary to gout is rare, patients with gouty arthritis of
the ankle can be treated via ankle fusion or replacement. Although recurrent gout flares
are theoretically a concern after ankle replacement, they are rare after knee
replacement. A small series showed good outcomes and few complications in patients
with end-stage gouty arthritis who underwent total ankle replacement, with no recurrent
gout flares over a mean follow-up 5.1 years.12
